hypotheses.claim: The newly introduced global AUDIT_TRACE_REGISTRY dict that stores raw bytes of each uploaded file causes unbounded memory growth, leading to the OOM kill.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: Code changes add a module‑level mutable dict and retain every upload's full byte payload without eviction. Metrics show RSS memory spiking to ~995 MB (EV-MET-001) and a strong positive correlation between memory and GC time (EV-MET-005). The number of concurrent uploads doubled (EV-MET-003), providing the data that populates the dict, which explains the rapid memory consumption observed in the logs (EV-LOG-001/002).
falsification_criteria: Memory usage does not increase when uploads are performed after the dict is cleared or the code is reverted to the version without the dict
The size of AUDIT_TRACE_REGISTRY remains constant (or empty) during a high‑load test while memory still reaches OOM levels
verification_plan: Instrument the service to expose the current length and total byte size of AUDIT_TRACE_REGISTRY during a load test
Run a synthetic upload workload matching the observed spike (≈15 concurrent uploads) and record memory usage and dict size
Revert the code to remove the global dict and repeat the same workload; verify that memory stays near baseline
Add an eviction/clear routine to the dict, trigger it during the test, and confirm that memory usage drops accordingly

hypotheses.claim: A sudden increase in concurrent upload requests saturated the container’s memory limit, causing the OOM kill independent of code changes.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: Logs record memory usage climbing to 85 % of the 1 GB container limit, then critical pressure at 990 MB, followed by a kernel OOM kill (EV-LOG-001‑004). Metrics confirm RSS rose to ~995 MB (EV-MET-001) and active uploads jumped to 15 (EV-MET-003), indicating the workload itself could exhaust memory even without the new dict.
falsification_criteria: Running the same upload volume on the previous code version does not cause memory to approach the container limit
Reducing the number of concurrent uploads below the observed spike prevents memory from reaching OOM thresholds
verification_plan: Deploy the prior version of the service (without the global dict) in an identical container configuration
Generate controlled upload traffic matching the 15‑upload spike and monitor container memory
Gradually increase/decrease concurrent uploads to identify the threshold at which memory pressure becomes critical
Confirm that OOM events only occur when the upload concurrency exceeds the identified threshold

hypotheses.claim: The GC pause time explosion indicates a pathological garbage‑collection behavior that prevented memory reclamation, contributing to the OOM condition.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: GC pause time jumped from a baseline of ~4.6 ms to 520 ms (EV-MET-002) exactly when RSS memory spiked (EV-MET-001). A very high Pearson correlation (r≈0.90) between RSS and GC time (EV-MET-005) suggests that as memory grew, GC struggled, likely retaining large objects (e.g., the stored byte payloads). This GC inefficiency could have accelerated the OOM event.
falsification_criteria: Enabling detailed GC logs shows short pause times despite high memory usage after the dict is removed
Forcing a full GC during the high‑memory period successfully reclaims a large portion of RSS, indicating GC was not the bottleneck
verification_plan: Enable Python GC debugging flags in the service and capture pause durations under load with the current code
Perform the same load with the global dict removed and compare GC pause statistics
Trigger an explicit full garbage collection (gc.collect()) during the high‑memory phase and measure reclaimed memory
Analyze heap profiles to identify object types that dominate memory before and after the dict removal

proposals.summary: Remove the global AUDIT_TRACE_REGISTRY dict and stop storing raw upload bytes in memory.
proposals.rationale: The unbounded growth of AUDIT_TRACE_REGISTRY caused each upload's full byte payload to remain in memory, leading to OOM; removing the dict eliminates the memory leak while preserving the functional behavior of returning the file size.
